section.title: Linear approximation in applications
section.p: Optimization asked for the best choice. Related rates asked how fast quantities change together.
If the input is a little wrong, how wrong is the output?
A radius may be measured only to the nearest millimeter. An angle may be off by one degree. A price model may be only an approximation. Calculus gives a first answer through the tangent line.
The derivative is the multiplier that turns a small input change into a small output change.
That is the practical meaning of the derivative in this section.

subsection.title: Sensitivity in measurement
subsection.p: A large value of |f'(x)| means that a small input error can create a large output error. A small value of |f'(x)| means the output is less sensitive to input error.

note.title: Sensitivity
note.p: For y=f(x), the size of |f'(x)| tells how strongly errors in x are amplified into errors in y.

subsection.p: Linear approximation gives us three related calculations:
subsection.md: \text{estimate output change} \amp:\amp \Delta y\approx f'(x)\Delta x, \\ \text{estimate input change} \amp:\amp \Delta x\approx \dfrac{\Delta y}{f'(x)}, \\ \text{estimate sensitivity} \amp:\amp \left|\dfrac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}\right|\approx |f'(x)|.
subsection.p: So far we have mostly used the first and third. The second one is about to become a method for solving equations.
If f(x) is not zero, how far should we move x so that f(x) becomes zero? The tangent line gives the first guess. Repeating that guess gives Newton's method.
